item.title: Focusing on the “T” (Therapy) in CBT for Adult ADHD
item.description:
ADHD

Focusing on the “T” (Therapy) in CBT for Adult ADHD

Tailoring evidence-based therapy for ADHD and everything that comes with it.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-supported, non-medical treatment for adult ADHD.
  • CBT often must be adapted to address co-existing psychiatric or medical diagnoses and various life stressors.
  • Basic familiarity with ADHD is necessary to adequately adapt CBT for adult ADHD.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-supported psychosocial treatment for adult ADHD. There are several available treatment manuals for clinicians, some with corresponding client workbooks. There is also a batch of other options tied to the credible, effective principles that guide treatments for adults with ADHD.

The most respected manuals have research support, chiefly via randomized controlled trials (RCTs), considered the ideal means to establish that a treatment works as promised.1 A necessary facet of these RCTs is identifying participants who have ADHD without co-existing diagnoses to ensure the treatments are, in fact, directly addressing and improving the symptoms of ADHD.

When ADHD Gets Complicated—Which Is Usually

Here is where the discussion of the “T,” the “therapy in CBT, arises2, and it's particularly relevant for adult ADHD. It’s well established that many things travel alongside ADHD, some of the most common being other psychiatric diagnoses, learning differences, and substance use issues.

However, these formal categories do not touch on the many life stressors that affect and are affected by ADHD, such as dealing with other health issues, such as diabetes, sensory or mobility ailments, reproductive health, caring for aging parents, pending divorce, or food scarcity. Even positive events can be stressful and difficult to navigate, such as marriage, raising children, a work promotion, or bringing home a puppy.

Adapting CBT for Adult ADHD

CBT for complex cases of adult ADHD requires individual treatment blueprints while using tried-and-true evidence-based principles for adult ADHD.
Source: Tima Miroshnichenko/Pexels

Some of the best RCT-based CBT manuals for adult ADHD present a series of 12 to 14 sessions or so, with session-by-session objectives and skill practice between sessions. This ensures that participants get an adequate “dose” of specialized psychosocial adult ADHD treatment. Thus, they are ready for use by clinicians in the community outside the structure of research.

However, their use with free-range adults with ADHD requires some “flexible rigor” by clinicians to adapt and personalize them to the individual needs of each client. The session-by-session approach provides guidance for the essential topics. You could think of the manuals as providing the piano keyboard and the notes, but clinical practice requires different tunes for different clients while still hitting all the keys.

Some manualized approaches draw on a conceptualization-based approach to adult ADHD, tailoring the presentation of the same CBT principles used in modular approaches at the outset and throughout treatment.3 Yet, there are no trade secrets about the necessary coping skills for managing and living well with adult ADHD.

Adapting CBT Requires Understanding ADHD

Basic familiarity with and understanding of the nature of ADHD and its effects is necessary. Unfortunately, very few practicing clinicians have received any formal training in the assessment and treatment of adult ADHD, either in the classroom or through supervised clinical experience in graduate and medical training programs.4 This lack of experience may contribute to rigid, inflexible administration of CBT for adult ADHD without adequate tailoring to individual clients, which has contributed to poor outcomes reported in a recent study. In the same study, a client who worked with an ADHD-familiar clinician described his positive experience as “transformative.”5

CBT for Adult ADHD Beyond Symptoms

A recent comprehensive meta-analysis of a batch of studies of CBT for adult ADHD yielded some encouraging results.6 The review focused on clinical research in which the outcome measures focused on improved overall functioning and quality of life, as well as functioning within specific domains of life, such as work, academics, and relationships.

The results showed that CBT for adult ADHD has many positive effects for overall life functioning, not just symptoms. Workplace functioning showed the strongest positive effects; social life, academics, and overall quality of life had more modest, sometimes inconsistent positive results. The modest results in these areas might reflect the great variability in social life and types of schooling.

Nevertheless, CBT for adult ADHD has some core principles that are beneficial and lend themselves to being adapted to the needs of individual clients. At the same time, future studies may examine CBT approaches specifically tailored to these different life domains as well as some of the other life stressors that complicate life with adult ADHD.

item.title: The Resilience Trap
item.description:
Resilience

The Resilience Trap

Your exhaustion may be a design flaw, not a personal failing.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • When exhaustion is widespread, it reflects how work and life are designed, not personal weakness.
  • When effort never changes conditions, people can learn to stop trying.
  • Real resilience requires redesigning systems instead of simply training individuals to tolerate them.
Source: Anton Popov/Adobe Stock

During World War II, B-17 bombers kept belly-landing because pilots were pressing the wrong switch. On the face of things, it looked like pilot error. Then a young psychologist named Alphonse Chapanis observed that two switches—one for the landing flaps and the other for the landing gear—sat next to each other and looked the same. A pilot worn out by hours of combat could easily reach for the wrong one as he came in to land. So Chapanis fitted a small wheel to the gear lever and a flap-shaped wedge to the flap control.

The confusion largely disappeared.

Most of us aren’t flying bombers, but we do live in a world in which nothing feels settled. Technology, work, the economy, politics, and the institutions we once trusted are all shifting at once. This breeds exhaustion and burnout. When people struggle, we prescribe resilience training. When the news becomes unbearable, we suggest a digital detox.

In effect, we keep telling the pilots to be more careful. But what if the problem isn’t the pilots at all but the system around them? What if rather than people failing to adapt to the world we have built, the world we have built is failing to account for the people who must live in it?

Exhaustion Is a System Output

When one person gets burnout, it makes sense to send them to a doctor. But when exhaustion shows up across entire workforces, professions, and generations, it is time to look at system design. As burnout experts Christina Maslach and Michael Leiter point out, over 20 years of research suggests that working conditions are one of the most important factors in causing burnout.

If exhaustion were mainly an individual problem, we would expect individual fixes to show some effect. But a study that surveyed 46,336 workers in 233 UK organizations found that those who took part in resilience training, mindfulness programs, or well-being apps appeared no better off than those who didn't. Interventions at the systemic level, concluded the author, seemed more important for employee well-being than programs targeted at helping individuals cope. It is a snapshot, not a trial, but the pattern is striking.

Resilience, in other words, is something environments help produce. As the developmental psychologist Ann Masten says, resilience should be seen not as a personality trait but as a capacity that is produced by relationships, communities, and supportive systems. If your job demands 70-hour weeks with no end in sight, it does not matter how many resilience workshops you attend. You are going to burn out.

I wrote a book called Reinvent, so I don’t say this lightly: Reinvention has a cost. Reinventing ourselves to pursue a meaningful possibility can energize us. Being forced to reinvent again and again because the ground never stops moving wears us down. Change is inevitable. Making people feel perpetually destabilized is a design choice.

The Resilience Trap

Early research pioneered by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier showed that repeated exposure to outcomes we cannot influence undermines our motivation to act. Subsequent work sharpened this finding, showing that passivity is a default human response to prolonged adversity. Control, it turns out, is a behavior that must be learned.

Now think about what individual resilience training asks of an exhausted employee. It tells her that the answer to her struggles lies in her own hands. She is responsible for managing her stress, reframing her thinking, and building her mental toughness. In pursuit of these goals, she attends the right workshops, gets up each morning to do her prescribed meditation, and maintains her gratitude journal with both dedication and devotion.

But when Monday morning comes, the workload is the same, the deadlines are the same, and the next reorganization is already on its way.

She has made the effort demanded of her, and yet nothing has changed. Then it happens again, and again, and again. Each round or reinvention denies her the one experience that might build the sense that she is truly in control of her situation: effort that pays off.

So she stops trying. She stops speaking up, stops suggesting fixes, and silently disengages from the practices demanded of a “good” employee. Her managers see this and call it apathy. They may even prescribe more resilience training.

Building Real Resilience

If that story sounds familiar—if you are the one feeling exhausted—the question to ask is not “What is wrong with me?” but rather “What are the conditions that keep producing this situation?” That question won’t change the conditions by itself, but it does lift the self-blame that tends to come with the feeling that events are slipping outside one’s own control. The next critical step is to make distinctions between information and influence, recognizing that awareness is not the same thing as agency.

Because the problem is systemic, the solution has to be too. Much of what exhausts people today was designed into existence, which means it is not immutable; it can be fixed by intentional redesign. Here are four changes leaders can make now.

  1. Involve people before decisions, not after. Communication after a decision is not the same as participation before it. When people help shape a change, their effort influences the outcome, which is exactly the experience that builds a sense of control.
  2. Close the loop. When someone raises a problem, act on it immediately when you can, and tell them what changed because they spoke up. Even a small fix shows people, in the plainest possible way, that their effort makes a difference. That is the experience the resilience trap takes away.
  3. Pair every new demand with a new resource. If a team is asked to take on more, it should also get something: time, people, training, or permission to stop doing something else. As the job demands-resources model shows, exhaustion grows when demands outpace resources. A demand without a resource is just a heavier load.
  4. Measure the conditions, not just the mood. Engagement scores tell you that people have checked out, but not why. Track the things that wear people down: workload, the pace of change, how often people get a say in decisions that affect them. That way, you are inspecting the cockpit instead of blaming the pilot.

A World Worth Adapting To

Those B-17 pilots needed better switches, not more grit.

To be clear, individual traits matter. They help us face the hardships no one can prevent. But strength of character should never become a way of making people carry the hardships we could prevent.

For years, we have asked people to adapt to the systems we build. It is time to build systems that adapt to people.

item.title: Is Your Adult Child In Crisis, or Are You Too Anxious?
item.description:
Parenting

Is Your Adult Child In Crisis, or Are You Too Anxious?

How parents can learn to stop mistaking struggles for actual danger.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • When your own anxiety takes over, it's hard to distinguish your adult child's struggles from true danger.
  • Slowing down to ask a crucial question can help you tell the difference between distress and danger.
  • Empathy helps you calm yourself and your adult child and supports them in learning how to self-advocate.

You hear the tone or see your phone light up as you get a text or a call from your struggling adult child. Either way, alarms go off in your head, and I'm talking really loud alarms. Many parents in this situation wrestle with what to think and how to react.

Just the other day, I conducted a parent coaching session with Lisa, who has a 29-year-old daughter, Casey (names changed to protect privacy). They are a perfect example of that hypervigilant state of mind so present in parents of struggling adult children. Feeling an inner sensation of her blood pressure rising, Lisa tells herself to "just listen" when her phone lights up with Casey's call.

During that hair-raising call, Casey right away starts pouring out, "I hate my friggin' job." (The f-word that was actually spoken is changed here.) Casey continues, "Like seriously, Mom, my boss hates me and is giving me lots of crap. I can't take it anymore, Mom, I'm like falling apart."

So Much for Just Listening When Your Anxious Voice Is Inwardly Screaming

As Lisa is willing herself to "just listen" to Casey, she is distracted by loud alarms going off in her mind. Her racing thoughts include, "Should I call her brother who lives across town to check on her?" Or, "Ugh, hmm...maybe I should offer to send her money and tell her to quit." These thoughts gain momentum and traction as they race around in Lisa’s mind.

At our previous coaching session a week before this call, when Lisa shared her thought patterns about Casey—which, as she sounded out, were clearly overthinking loops—something changed for her. Lisa gained insight in a way she never had before, which she applied in this call with Casey. In the words of physician and poet Oliver Wendell Holmes, “A moment's insight is sometimes worth a life's experience." Let's now look at the magic question Lisa asked herself to gain calm and clarity.

A Crucial Question for Any Anxious Parent Tempted to Jump In Too Fast

For some context here, Lisa and I had practiced having her ask herself several helpful questions in the face of those maddening, overthinking-laden thoughts that had been consuming her about Casey. So during that same phone call, when Lisa reflexively heard Casey, seemingly in crisis, she asked herself a question that helped her slow down: "Is Casey in danger, or is she distressed?" That question helped Lisa realize, "Well, hold on, nothing really bad has actually happened; Casey is just really upset right now."

Clearly, Casey being upset and Casey actually being in a life-altering crisis are not the same thing. Sure, Casey was stressed, felt trapped at work, and was acutely feeling that she hated her job. But Lisa realized that all those things could be going on without her needing to help Casey escape the situation.

As I discuss in my book The Rescue Trap: How well-meaning parents keep their adult children stuck, many parents don’t know how to step back and reappraise these situations. Too often, they hear what sounds like sirens, slip on their first responder uniforms, and then unwittingly give their adult child the message, “You can’t handle life on your own without me.”

A Better Plan: Use Empathy to Bring In Calm and Clarity

Let's go back one last time to that "distress call" from Casey. Instead of immediately trying to rescue her daughter, Lisa asked herself if Casey was struggling or in a true crisis, and then said to her, “That sounds really hard. I can hear how overwhelmed you are. Do you want me just to listen, or would it help to think through some options?”

Can you see how the shift that Lisa made really matters? Think about it: With that response, Lisa was still caring, and she was still emotionally present for Casey. Lisa, for sure, did not become cold, detached, or dismissive. Rather, she resisted the urge to turn Casey’s distress into her own emergency. This was a huge victory for Lisa because she realized that for too long she was mistaking Casey's struggles for emergencies that she had to eradicate.

Final Thoughts

When your adult child is hurting, your nervous system may start telling you that you have to do something right now. That inner voice screams, "Fix this, or send money, or make a call" on behalf of your adult child (e.g., call their landlord). But do you really want to risk sending the problematic, unintended message: “I don’t think you can handle this on your own”?
